About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Chemistry Years 12–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Chemistry Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Chemistry Years 12–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Chemistry Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12 from
1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  Students are taught about the properties, structure, and composition of matter,
  and the physical and chemical transformations it undergoes. They are taught how
  to investigate chemical systems and processes through theoretical knowledge
  and practical applications.

Through the study of Chemistry students are taught how matter behaves, changes,
and interacts, and how these understandings are used to interpret natural processes
and human-designed systems. By integrating Chemistry knowledge with quantitative
reasoning, sustainability considerations, and ethical decision-making, Chemistry
supports learners to engage with real-world issues and to contribute thoughtfully to
solutions that affect people and the natural world.

Chemistry, provides students with the knowledge and practices to learn how matter
behaves, changes, and interacts, and how these understandings are used to interpret
natural processes and human-designed systems. They are also taught disciplinary
knowledge that enables them to evaluate scientific claims, explanations, methods,
and applications using evidence and scientific criteria.

As students' progress through Chemistry, they are supported to develop increasingly
sophisticated abilities in using chemical concepts, terminology, models, and theories
to describe the structure, properties, and behaviour of matter, and to understand how
chemical knowledge is produced, organised, and applied.

  Years 12–13 Chemistry provides a foundation for success across a range of
  subjects including chemistry and related sciences, biology, physics, biomedical
  science, medicine, environmental science, engineering, biotechnology, and
  health sciences.

Investigating in science

Scientists develop meaningful questions and use investigations to explain
phenomena. They gather or select evidence (collect primary data or source
secondary data) analyse data, identify patterns and relationships, evaluate evidence,
consider alternative explanations, and distinguish between strong and weak support
for claims. Scientists test theories by attempting to falsify them rather than prove
them.

At Years 12 and 13, students continue to investigate scientific questions, gather and
analyse evidence, and use this evidence to explain scientific phenomena and develop
their understanding of Chemistry.

Opportunities should be provided each year for students to undertake both practical
and secondary-source investigations, working independently, and collaboratively.

Contexts and investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and
interests of students, their community, and the local environment.

Delivery of Year 12 and 13 Chemistry programmes must align with Safety and
Science | Pūtaiao guidance.

Further guidance on programme design, investigation opportunities, and resource
selection is available in the Chemistry Curriculum Support Document.
